rationale: Complex coadaptations are explained by heritable variation and selection, not by direct climatic or nutritional induction alone. External conditions can influence development, but do not adequately account for the coordinated structures described.

Overproduction and finite resources commonly generate differential survival or reproduction, and beneficial heritable variants tend to increase. The wording understates reproduction and inheritance, but captures natural selection's core logic.

Selection can drive competitive replacement, extinction, and ecological divergence, but none is almost inevitable in every lineage. Drift, environmental change, coexistence, and stabilizing selection are also important.

Common descent and species change are overwhelmingly supported. The claim that same-genus species descend from a single generally extinct species is broadly phylogenetic, though genera are artificial and can be non-monophyletic.

Natural selection is a major cause of adaptive modification, alongside drift, mutation, gene flow, developmental processes, and sexual selection. Calling it the main cause across all organic change is broad but defensible for adaptation.

Artificial selection has produced striking variation within many domestic breeds and cultivars. The universal comparison with any wild species or variety is too strong, and domestication can also reduce genetic diversity through bottlenecks.

Changed environments can alter phenotypes and selection, but domestic diversity primarily reflects mutation, recombination, hybridization, artificial selection, and population history. Less uniform living conditions are not a general sufficient explanation.

Most inherited variability originates from mutation and recombination rather than reproductive elements being altered by preconception living conditions. Environmental mutagenesis and epigenetic inheritance occur, but are not the most frequent general cause.

Ordinary use and disuse do not generally produce inherited anatomical changes. Duck skeletal differences are better explained by genetic selection and developmental plasticity than inheritance of acquired effects.

Traits often share developmental and genetic bases, so selection on one character commonly causes correlated responses in others. 'Almost certainly' is stronger than warranted because some selected traits are relatively independent.

Many age-specific genetic effects and developmental traits recur at corresponding life stages in offspring. However, the age at which a novel parental peculiarity first appeared is not itself generally encoded or inherited.

Domestic races and closely related species commonly differ through the same kinds of quantitative and morphological variation, with breeds usually less diverged and more interfertile. Monstrous traits and variable uniformity make the comparison imperfect.

Many wild species could respond strongly to prolonged domestication and selection, but domesticated taxa were nonrandomly chosen for tractability, reproduction, and useful variation. Equal average variability is therefore unsupported.

Genomic evidence indicates that domestic dogs derive principally from an ancient wolf population, with later introgression from wolves and other canids. This is not descent from several distinct wild species in the ordinary sense.
Genetic, behavioral, and morphological evidence strongly supports the rock dove as the source of domestic pigeon breeds. Geographic lineages and later admixture do not undermine that origin.

Most breed and cultivar differentiation reflects cumulative artificial selection on standing and new variation, often augmented by crossing. Some traits arose through large-effect mutations, but present useful forms were generally assembled over generations.

Directional artificial selection produces the largest divergence in targeted organs and traits. Correlated responses and genome-wide differences mean other parts need not remain only slightly changed.

Preferential breeding from valued individuals can shift traits substantially even without an explicit redesign goal. 'Any breed' and guaranteed improvement are too universal, since response depends on heritable variation and what counts as improvement.

Domestication can make crops morphologically unlike their progenitors, and several crop origins were historically difficult to identify. Missing or extinct wild populations, hybridization, and incomplete evidence also contribute, so accumulated change is not the sole explanation.

Selection by humans has often emphasized visible morphology, producing dramatic external diversity among breeds. Internal physiology, behavior, and anatomy have also been strongly selected, so the general contrast has important exceptions.
Larger populations sample more mutations and recombinants and therefore increase the chance of a desired heritable variant. This is a standard population-genetic advantage in artificial selection.

Cumulative intentional and unintentional selection is the dominant explanation for most distinctive domestic traits. Hybridization, drift, bottlenecks, plasticity, and relaxed selection can dominate particular traits or populations.
Heritable variation among individuals is the essential substrate of natural selection, just as it is for artificial selection. Modern genetics strongly supports this principle.

Neutral or nearly neutral variation can remain polymorphic, consistent with the claim. Yet high variation in these genera can also reflect polyploidy, hybridization, apomixis, population structure, and selection, and neutrality of the structures is not established.

Gene flow in mobile sexual animals tends to erase local differentiation, while geographic separation promotes ambiguous stages of speciation. Nonetheless hybrid zones, clines, and locally adapted forms provide substantial within-country exceptions.

Evolution produces continua of divergence, and taxonomic ranks below and at species level have unavoidable borderline cases. Some species are sharply delimited, but no universal threshold separates all these categories.

Selection can accumulate differences and turn populations or varieties into reproductively isolated species. Speciation is not a compulsory linear sequence and also depends on drift, gene flow, chromosomal change, and ecological history.

Species boundaries and taxonomic conventions can be fuzzy, especially during divergence, and the rank is partly conventional. Species nevertheless often correspond to biologically meaningful independently evolving lineages, making 'arbitrary' and no essential difference too sweeping.

Widespread and abundant plant species often contain more recognized intraspecific variation because of large populations and environmental breadth. The relationship is not universal and is influenced by taxonomy, dispersal, mating systems, and sampling.

The tendency for large genera to contain proportionally more variable species has empirical support in some floras and is related to taxonomic and diversification patterns. It is not an invariant law across regions and clades.

Fossil and phylogenetic records show repeated radiation of initially small clades and decline or disappearance of formerly diverse genera. Taxonomic genus boundaries are conventional, but the macroevolutionary pattern is commonplace.

Clades with high past diversification may retain traits that promote current diversification, creating some correlation. Diversification rates vary through time and often slow or reverse, so many species having formed does not imply many are still forming.

Species-rich genera often include recent radiations whose members are morphologically very similar. However, genus delimitation and species recognition create strong ascertainment effects, and large genera can also encompass deep divergence.

Phylogenetic branching naturally creates nested clusters of more and less closely related species within large genera. The notion of species orbiting particular species is imprecise, but unequal clustering is expected and observed.

Recently diverged or narrowly differentiated species are often geographic isolates with small ranges. Range size is controlled by many ecological and historical factors, so close relatedness does not generally guarantee restriction.

Nested similarities, uneven divergence, and geographic patterns follow naturally from branching descent and population divergence. Independent creation has no scientific mechanism that predicts these linked regularities.

Some species-rich clades continue radiating and successful lineages can generate many descendants. Diversity dependence, extinction, ecological limits, and shifting environments frequently prevent larger genera or dominant forms from becoming ever more dominant.

Potential population growth generally exceeds realized survival, producing competition, predation, disease, or environmental mortality. Density independence can occur temporarily, but long-run population limitation is unavoidable.

Released from enemies or constraints, introduced populations can grow exponentially without any evolved increase in individual fertility. Some invasions also involve evolution, repeated introduction, or changed reproduction, so the exclusive wording is not universal.

Equilibrium abundance is set by survival, resources, interactions, and life history, not fecundity alone; high reproductive output often offsets high juvenile mortality. In some systems fecundity directly limits recruitment, so 'all cases' would be too strong.

Predators often regulate prey below food-limited carrying capacity, and trophic control is well documented. Resource limitation is also extremely common, making the broad comparative claim that predation more often determines abundance uncertain.

Extreme cold and drought can cause major episodic mortality and population bottlenecks. Across all taxa, resource limitation, disease, predation, competition, and ordinary climate can be equally or more effective, so 'most effective of all' is unsupported.

Species richness generally decreases poleward and under harsher high-elevation conditions, reducing some biotic interactions, while direct climatic stress often produces stunting. Elevational richness is frequently hump-shaped and biotic limitation remains important in cold regions.

Biotic interactions strongly mediate climatic range limits, and many cultivated exotics survive without naturalizing. Direct physiological climate constraints are nevertheless major for many species, and failure to naturalize can also reflect propagule limitation.

Positive density dependence, predator satiation, cooperative defense, and mate limitation can impose minimum viable densities, and local abundance with regional rarity is common. The proposed enemy-relative mechanism is only one of many and is not necessary in most cases.

Communities can exhibit long periods of approximate composition despite continual demographic turnover and can shift after small perturbations near thresholds. Many communities also show directional succession and substantial baseline change, so finely balanced uniformity is not general.

Indirect trophic and mutualistic cascades can link predators, rodents, pollinators, and plants, and such chains are well established. The direction and strength of the specific historical cat-to-clover pathway are context dependent.

Conspecifics often overlap most strongly in resource use and experience strong density dependence. Competition can be stronger between species under limiting-resource asymmetries, and predation or mutualism may matter more than competition, making 'almost always' excessive.
Closely related species tend to share niches, so competition is often stronger among congeners. Ecological divergence among relatives and convergence among distant taxa create many exceptions.

Natural selection shapes many organismal structures through competition, predation, and other species interactions, often in cryptic ways. 'Every organism' and essential relation to all relevant organisms overstate the case because abiotic selection and drift also shape structure.

Biotic interactions influence many range limits, but direct thermal and hydric tolerances commonly set poleward, elevational, and arid boundaries. Evidence does not support climate alone killing only a few range-edge species.

Heritable variants that improve reproductive success tend to increase and strongly deleterious variants tend to be purged. Survival is only one component, selection is stochastic in finite populations, and mildly harmful alleles are not invariably eliminated.

Strictly neutral variants are not directly selected and can remain polymorphic through mutation and drift. They do not necessarily stay variable, since drift can fix or eliminate them, and linked selection can change their frequencies.

Adaptation is constrained and environment-dependent rather than perfect, and successful invasions demonstrate exploitable ecological opportunities in many regions. The assertion that introduced species establish in every country is stronger than needed and may have exceptions.

Background matching reduces detection by visual predators and is a classic, experimentally supported adaptation. Color can serve additional functions, but the stated examples plausibly receive protective benefits.

Stage-specific heritable variation allows selection to optimize larvae, juveniles, and adults partly independently. Genetic correlations and tradeoffs constrain such independent modification but do not negate it.

Strong male-male competition and specialized weapons are common under polygyny because reproductive success is highly skewed. Monogamous species can also fight intensely, and polygynous competition may instead emphasize displays or sperm competition.

Persistent mate preferences can drive evolutionary changes in male song and plumage through sexual selection. Sensory biases, male competition, ecology, and genetic constraints also influence the resulting ornaments.

Sexual selection is a leading explanation for sex-limited ornaments, weapons, and displays when ecological roles are similar. Sex-specific fecundity selection, predation, and genetic or hormonal constraints explain some dimorphism instead.

Reciprocal and sequential coevolution between flowers and pollinators is extensively supported, with selection favoring mutually compatible traits. Not every apparent match reflects strict pairwise coevolution, but the claimed mechanism is sound.

Selection commonly builds complex adaptations through cumulative small changes, but large-effect mutations, regulatory changes, hybridization, polyploidy, and chromosomal rearrangements can cause substantial sudden changes. Selection also acts on standing variation rather than only infinitesimal new modifications.

Crossing genetically differentiated strains often masks deleterious recessives and produces heterosis, while close inbreeding exposes recessive load and causes depression. Outbreeding depression and naturally selfing lineages are important exceptions.

Numerous plant and animal lineages reproduce by persistent selfing or asexuality, and some have done so over very many generations. Occasional outcrossing is beneficial in many lineages but is not an indispensable universal law.

Dioecy is disproportionately common among woody plants in many floras, and separation promotes outcrossing. The pattern varies strongly by geography and lineage, so 'across all plant orders' is too broad.

Larger populations generate and retain more mutations and combinations, increasing the supply of beneficial variants. The probability of fixation and efficacy of selection also depend on drift, linkage, and population structure.

Large areas usually support larger populations, more ecological opportunity, and more total speciation, while successful continental lineages may spread broadly. Per-lineage speciation can be rapid on islands, and competition does not reliably make large-area forms superior or more prolific.

Fresh waters contain notable relict and phylogenetically isolated taxa, but also rapid radiations and high extinction rates. Small total area does not imply uniformly weak competition or slow evolution, and basin isolation can accelerate diversification.
Selection can act rapidly and simultaneously on many species and traits, as observed in ecological time. Some evolutionary responses are slow or episodic, but 'always very slowly' is false.

Competitive or selective increases can reduce less fit forms, and small populations face elevated extinction risk. Areas are not literally fully stocked, declines have many causes, and rarity can persist without extinction or result from it rather than precede it.

Close relatives often compete strongly because of niche overlap, and replacement can accompany speciation or invasion. New lineages frequently coexist with relatives through geographic separation or niche differentiation, so extermination is not a general tendency.

Niche complementarity often lets functionally diverse communities capture more resources and support greater biomass or abundance. Diversity can also increase competition or have saturating effects, and 'greatest amount of life' lacks a single metric.

Local coexistence often reflects limiting similarity and niche differentiation, so very close competitors may exclude one another. Many diverse communities nevertheless contain numerous congeners, and phylogenetic distance is an imperfect proxy for ecological difference.

Introduced floras can be enriched for genera absent from the recipient region because phylogenetic novelty may reduce shared enemies or competition. Patterns vary among regions and residence histories, and many naturalized plants belong to already native-rich genera.

Anagenesis and competitive replacement can remove ancestral forms, while incomplete sampling makes transitions appear discontinuous. Ancestors can persist alongside descendants, and many intermediate populations disappear through drift or environmental change rather than improvement.

Fossils frequently combine ancestral and derived features and occupy phylogenetic positions between major living lineages. Fossil sampling is uneven and many extinct forms are specialized side branches, so not all are intermediates.
